objectives: Explain how consumption choices affect resource use and waste, and connect this to opportunity cost.
Explain why the cost an individual pays (private cost) can differ from the cost borne by society as a whole (social cost).
Compare the effects and limits of tools that encourage sustainable consumption (information, prices and deposits, and reuse).

concepts.definition: Consumption that meets today's needs while using fewer resources and creating less waste, so that resources remain for future generations. SDG 12 aims to ensure sustainable consumption and production patterns.

Every choice to buy or throw something away carries an opportunity cost: the other uses of that money or those resources that are given up. Wasted food has an opportunity cost when more is produced or bought than is used: the resources that went into the extra food could have been used for something else. Once food is made, the cost of making it is sunk, and the remaining choice is how to use it, such as eating it or donating it instead of throwing it away.

Private cost is the cost a consumer or producer pays directly. Social cost is the private cost plus the external costs that other people or future generations must bear (such as waste disposal and pollution). When the marginal social cost of an item is higher than the marginal private cost that buyers and sellers face, a market tends to produce and consume more than the socially efficient quantity.
Benefits or costs that change people's choices. Prices, deposits, discounts, fines, information, and social reputation can all act as incentives.

People care about more than money; they also value the environment and other people, and habits and convenience also shape their choices. Accurate information and awareness help people make more sustainable choices.

beginner.summary: What we buy, use, and throw away affects resources and waste. Knowing that some costs are paid by someone other than you can help you make better choices.

sections.heading: Throwing things away has a cost, too
paragraphs: When you leave part of your school cafeteria lunch uneaten, you're not just throwing away food. The water, electricity, and work used to grow, transport, and cook that food are thrown away with it. When more food is made than is eaten, those resources could have been used for something else, so wasted food has an opportunity cost. Once a lunch is made, the remaining choice is whether it gets eaten, shared, or thrown away. Sustainable consumption means meeting your needs while using fewer resources and creating less waste, for example by buying only what you need, using things for a long time, and reusing them.

sections.heading: Costs you don't pay
paragraphs: When a store gives you a free plastic bag, you don't pay anything. But someone has to collect and dispose of that bag, and if it ends up in the ocean, other people and future generations pay to clean it up. When the cost you pay is lower than the full cost to society, people tend to use more of that item than is best for society.

sections.heading: Small reasons that change choices
paragraphs: Charging for bags, giving money back when you return a cup (a deposit), or offering a discount when you bring your own cup all change people's choices. These are called incentives. And people don't think only about money. Caring about the environment, what friends think, and accurate information can change choices, too.

intermediate.summary: Consumption choices carry the opportunity cost of resources, and when the social cost of an item is higher than the private cost people pay, they tend to consume more than is socially efficient. Incentives such as prices, deposits, and information, along with people's values, change their choices.

sections.heading: Consumption and resources
paragraphs: Sustainable consumption is not just about using less; it is about getting the same satisfaction from fewer resources. The targets of SDG 12 include the efficient use of natural resources (12.2), halving per capita food waste at the retail and consumer levels and reducing food losses along production and supply chains (12.3), reducing waste generation (12.5), and information and awareness for sustainable lifestyles (12.8). Wasted food and goods represent other uses of the resources that went into producing them, so they are an opportunity cost for society as a whole.

sections.heading: Private cost and social cost
paragraphs: When a transaction imposes costs (such as waste or pollution) on third parties who are not part of the transaction, those costs are not included in the price. Consumers then decide based only on their private cost. Because the cost to society is higher than the cost they face, they tend to use more than the socially efficient amount. This kind of third-party effect is called an externality, and you will study it in detail in the market failure course (c03).

sections.heading: Incentives and policy tools
paragraphs: Policies change choices by changing incentives. Bag fees and similar charges raise private cost closer to social cost. Deposit-return systems pay people back when they return containers, increasing the share of containers collected for reuse or recycling. Disclosure and labeling (for example, publishing how much food waste is generated) let people choose knowing the consequences. Because people weigh environmental and social values alongside money, and habits matter a great deal, price tools are often combined with information and social-norm tools.

advanced.summary: When marginal social cost is higher than marginal private cost, the market tends to overconsume. Price tools (fees and deposits) and information and norm-based tools that close this gap each have different effects and limits. Whether reuse pays off depends on how many times an item is used.

sections.heading: Efficiency and sustainability in resource use
paragraphs: Getting the same utility from fewer resources is an efficiency gain; sustainability adds a further criterion: whether the choice narrows the options available to future generations. Reducing food waste lets us make fuller use of food already produced, which has an effect similar to increasing supply without increasing production (this connects to the SDG case in c02 Lesson 3).

sections.heading: The gap between private cost and social cost
paragraphs: Marginal social cost = marginal private cost + marginal external cost. Consumers consider only their own marginal private cost: they buy another unit when its marginal benefit is greater than its marginal private cost and stop where the two are equal. When there is an external cost, marginal social cost is higher than marginal private cost at that quantity, so they use more than the socially efficient quantity, where marginal benefit equals marginal social cost. If the price already covers the marginal private cost, a fee equal to the marginal external cost at the efficient quantity raises the price consumers face to the marginal social cost, so use falls to the efficient quantity. However, external costs are hard to measure precisely, and an equity concern remains: such fees can weigh relatively more heavily on low-income households.

sections.heading: Comparing tools and the reality of behavior
paragraphs: Because a deposit is refunded on return, it can raise collection rates while keeping the final burden on consumers small, but return facilities and administration are costly. Information and labeling are inexpensive but may have small effects and can lose out to habit and convenience. Because habits and convenience shape many choices and many people simply accept the default option, changing the default (for example, providing disposable cutlery only on request) is another design option.

Reusable items take more resources to make than single-use ones, so they pay off only if used enough times. The break-even number of uses can be estimated as the extra cost of the reusable item ÷ the net cost saved per use (the single-use cost avoided minus any washing or upkeep cost per use).

worked_examples.title: The value of a wasted cafeteria lunch
worked_examples.problem: Hypothetical example: The ingredients for one school cafeteria lunch cost $3, and a student usually leaves 30% of it uneaten. How much money's worth of ingredients is thrown away per meal?
worked_examples.answer: $0.90 worth (90 cents). The water, electricity, and labor used to grow, transport, and cook the ingredients are thrown away, too. This opportunity cost arises because more food was made than was eaten; once the lunch is made, the remaining choice is only how it is used.

worked_examples.title: How many uses until a reusable cup pays off?
worked_examples.problem: Hypothetical example: Suppose a café builds 10 cents for each disposable cup into the price of a drink and takes those 10 cents off when you bring your own cup. If you buy a $12 reusable cup, how many times must you use it to earn back its price? (Ignore washing costs.)
steps: Cost of the reusable cup: $12 = 1,200 cents.
worked_examples.answer: 120 uses. If you use it fewer times, you lose money, and the environmental benefit also appears only after enough uses.

worked_examples.title: Social cost and a bag fee
worked_examples.problem: Hypothetical example: Making one plastic bag costs 2 cents (private cost), and after use, collection, disposal, and environmental damage cost society another 3 cents (external cost, assumed value). (1) If stores give bags away for free, what is the gap between the social cost of one bag and the price the consumer pays? (2) If a store instead charges the 2-cent production cost, what additional fee per bag would make the price the consumer pays equal to the social cost?
steps: Social cost = private cost of 2 cents + external cost of 3 cents = 5 cents.
(1) If the bag is free, the consumer pays 0 cents → a gap of 5 − 0 = 5 cents.

(2) If the store charges the 2-cent production cost, the remaining gap is 5 − 2 = 3 cents, so an additional fee of 3 cents (equal to the external cost) makes the price 5 cents, equal to the social cost.
worked_examples.answer: (1) 5 cents. (2) An additional fee of 3 cents, for a total bag price of 2 + 3 = 5 cents, equal to the social cost.

real_world_examples.title: Pollution and social cost
paragraphs: When a factory releases pollution, the costs the factory pays directly (its private costs) do not include the harm suffered by people nearby. If the social cost, which includes that harm, is greater than the private cost, the market produces more of the product than is socially desirable.

real_world_examples.title: Choices that money alone can't explain
paragraphs: In economic models, acting in your own interest does not have to mean being selfish. People also value things like family, charity, and the environment, and these values enter into the benefits and costs of their choices.

sdg_case.title: Reducing food waste in our school cafeteria
paragraphs: SDG target 12.3 calls for halving per capita food waste at the retail and consumer levels and reducing food losses along production and supply chains.

Hypothetical scenario: A lot of food is left uneaten in your school cafeteria every day. The student council and the school's nutrition staff want to choose a way to reduce food waste. Compare how each option changes students' incentives and information, and what costs it involves.

options.name: Publish each class's food waste every week
benefits: Seeing the results motivates students to waste less on their own (information and social norms).
costs: Measuring and recording the waste takes staff time.
The effect may be small or fade quickly.
assumptions: Students pay attention to the published results and respond to them.

options.name: Let students choose their portion size (small, regular, or large)
benefits: Students take only what they will eat, so less is left over.
costs: Nutritional balance may get less attention.
assumptions: Students know how much food is right for them.

options.name: Reward classes whose food waste falls below a target
benefits: It creates a clear incentive to reduce waste.
costs: It may cause side effects, such as students forcing themselves to eat or secretly throwing food away.
assumptions: The rewards are attractive enough, and measurement is fair.

discussion: The three options change information, choice, and financial incentives, respectively. What combination would be most effective at your school, and what assumptions does that judgment rely on?

key_takeaways: Choices to consume and throw things away carry the opportunity cost of resources; sustainable consumption means getting the same satisfaction with fewer resources and less waste.
When the social cost of an item is higher than the private cost people pay (for example, because of waste or pollution), people tend to use more than the socially efficient amount.
Financial incentives such as prices and deposits, and approaches based on information, values, and habit design, each have strengths and limits, so they are often used together.
